For the sake of convenience, hereinafter parties shall be referred as per their original status i.e.
'appellant' as 'plaintiff' and 'respondents' as 'defendants'.
Averments in the plaint 4.

Plaintiff instituted a suit for permanent injunction before Ld. Court of Sub-Judge, Delhi on averments that he purchased a land out of khasra No.4 measuring 100 square yards in abadi of village Raipur Delhi (now known as Sanwal Nagar, New Delhi) (hereinafter referred as "suit property" or "suit land") from Shri Nav Dev, who sold the property to plaintiff through his attorney vide registered sale deed dated 29.07.1966.
5.

It is stated that when the plaintiff purchased the piece of land, the plots were not precisely demarcated/divided as it was agricultural land defined by khasra numbers only, and when the plots for the village were demarcated, plaintiff's piece of land was given plot no. C/37, as per the plan confirmed by DDA.
6.
Plaintiff averred that he constructed a house on the said plot, and house tax of the house was assessed by the MCD, which he was regularly paying to the MCD.

It is stated that after Page no.4 of 29 RCA DJ No. 3/2016 Kanhaiya Lal v. Khairati Lal & Others construction of the house on the plot,
he let out the house to the tenants for having rental income to meet expenses of his family.

sentences.text: Plaintiff stated that he was enjoying the possession of the property since then.

7. Plaintiff further stated that defendants no.1 to 5 were influential persons of the locality and were also having influence on the staff of MCD & DDA and without any reason, defendant no.2 to 5 attempted to dispossess the plaintiff from his house many times.
8.
On 27.06.1985, the defendants' hired men came to plaintiff's house and attempted to dispossess him from the suit property.

It is stated that plaintiff lodged a complaint with PS Defence Colony in this regard, but again on 27.07.1985, defendant no. 1 to 5, and an inspector of DDA came to the suit property and started throwing out materials belonging to the plaintiff, which were lying in the unconstructed portion.
9.

Thus, by way of the present suit, plaintiff prayed that the defendants be restrained from dispossessing him from the suit property i.e. built-up plot number C/37 House Number 70 C in 100 sq. yds. of khasra No.4 situated in Sanwal Nagar, New Delhi, without following due process of law.
Written Statements 10.
Defendant no. 1 to 5 contested the suit and filed their written statement.

It is stated that land in suit belonged to, and is in the Page no.5 of 29 RCA DJ No. 3/2016 Kanhaiya Lal v. Khairati Lal &
Others actual physical possession of, the Kohli Temple Trust, Sanwal Nagar having been donated to it by the original purchasers under a compromise between the Sanwal Nagar Welfare Association,
on the one hand, and the original purchasers Shri Budh Prakash and Shri Babu Lal, on the other,
arrived at in the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi.

sentences.text: It is stated that the Ld. Trial Court failed to appreciate that the plaintiff was in possession of the property, not in the capacity of trespasser who had illegally and unauthorizedly captured the land but had purchased the suit property vide registered sale deed from the previous owner.
28. It is further stated that the Ld. Trial Court committed grave error in holding that the suit property had been acquired by DDA as the DDA never took possession of the suit property.
The DDA failed to prove service of notice under the Land Acquisition Act or that they had taken possession under the said Act.
The award or its implementation has not been proved.
DDA has also not proved that it had paid any compensation to the rightful owner or fulfilled the requirements of acquiring the land.
DDA is not in possession of any part of the land in question and the same is in the ownership of various residents of the locality.
29. It is further stated that the Ld. Trial Court failed to record any finding as to possession of the plaintiff while deciding Issue no.2.
Both PW-1 and PW-2 proved their possession and respective titles in respect of the suit property.
The report of the Local Commissioner and the site plan have been proved by DW Yogender Gautam, Local Commissioner.
The report was not challenged by the defendants by filing any objections.

Thus, the possession of the plaintiff over the suit property is sufficiently proved by the evidence on record, which the Ld. Page no.10 of 29 RCA DJ No. 3/2016 Kanhaiya Lal v. Khairati Lal & Others Trial Court failed to appreciate.

31. Lastly, it is stated that Ld. Trial Court failed to appreciate that the plaintiff was in lawful possession of the suit property whereas the defendants were not in possession thereof.
By dismissing the suit, the Ld. Trial Court committed grave error in taking away the right of the plaintiff to protect its possession from unlawful actions of the defendants.

Analysis 45.
I have heard arguments on behalf of the parties and perused the record including the trial court record.

46. From a reading of the impugned judgment dated 25.04.2009, it is noted that the suit of the plaintiff was mainly dismissed on the ground that he was a rank trespasser and was not entitled to any injunction against the true owner.

My issue wise analysis is as follows:

47.

Issue No.2 Whether the plaintiff is in possession?

At the outset, it is pertinent to note that the Ld. Trial Court, in the impugned judgment, did not give any finding as to whether the plaintiff was or was not in possession of the suit property, and rather held that the plaintiff was a rank tress-passer who is not entitled to relief of possession.
49. It is the case of the plaintiff that he had purchased the suit property vide registered sale deed Ex PW2/A and came into possession of the suit property.
50. Plaintiff deposed that he had constructed upon the land after purchasing it, and let out the same to tenants.

Plaintiff deposed that he was assessed by the MCD for house tax and proved the receipts of the payment of the house tax as Ex.PW2/B to Ex.PW2/E.

sentences.text: DW1 though deposed that plaintiff had no right, title or interest in the suit property, he did not verify from the persons who were found in the possession of the said land as to who was claiming ownership of the said property.

DW1, as per his deposition visited the suit land about 3-4 days prior to recording of his evidence, but he did not ascertain the names of the persons residing there as tenants nor did he verify as to who was the landlord of the property.

55. This is also contrary to the case tried to be set up by defendant no. 6/DDA that the suit property is a vacant land, which suggestion was also categorically denied by PW-1 in the cross- examination by defendant no. 6/DDA.
56.

It is evident that not only the plaintiff but both the defendants' witnesses admitted that DDA was not in possession of the suit land rather it was found in possession of the plaintiff or some tenants.

73. It is pertinent to refer to the celebrated judgment of Rame Gowda (D) By Lrs vs M. Varadappa Naidu (D) By Lrs. & Anr. 2 wherein the Hon'ble Apex Court held as under:
"It is thus clear that so far as the Indian law is concerned the person in peaceful possession is entitled to retain his possession and in order to protect such possession he may even use reasonable force to keep out a trespasser.

sentences.text: A rightful owner who has been wrongfully dispossessed of land may retake possession if he can do so peacefully and without the use of unreasonable force.

If the trespasser is in settled possession of the property belonging to the rightful owner, the rightful owner shall have to take recourse to law; he cannot take the law in his own hands and evict the trespasser or interfere with his possession.

74 . It was further held that:
"In Munshi Ram & Ors.'s case (supra), it was held that no one, including the true owner, has a right to dispossess the trespasser by force if the trespasser is in settled possession of the land and in such a case unless he is evicted in the due course of law,
he is entitled to defend his possession even against the rightful owner.
But merely stray or even intermittent acts of trespass do not give such a right against the true owner.
The possession which a trespasser is entitled to defend against the rightful owner must be settled possession, extending over a sufficiently long period of time and acquiesced to by the true owner.
A casual act of possession would not have the effect of interrupting the possession of the rightful owner.
The rightful owner may re-enter and re- instate himself provided he does not use more force than is necessary.
Such entry will be viewed only as resistance to an intrusion upon his possession which has never been lost.
A stray act of trespass, or a possession which has not matured into settled possession, can be obstructed or removed by the true owner even by using necessary force.
In Puran Singh and Ors.'s case (supra), the Court clarified that it is difficult to lay down any hard and fast rule as to when the possession of a trespasser can mature into settled possession.

The 'settled possession'
must be (i) effective, (ii) undisturbed, and (iii) to the knowledge of the owner or without any attempt at concealment by the trespasser.

In the cases of Munshi Ram and Ors.(supra) and Puran Singh and Ors. (supra), the Court has approved the statement of law made in Horam Vs. Nevertheless, he has been found to be in settled possession of the property.
Even the defendant failed in proving his title over the disputed land so as to substantiate his entitlement to evict the plaintiff.

The Trial Court and the High Court have rightly decided the suit.

Ex.PW2/1 is a duly registered document, pursuant to which plaintiff came into possession of the suit property.
The house-tax receipts Ex. PW2/C to Ex. PW2/E, report of Local Commissioner Ex. DW1/1, testimony of DW-1 and revenue records Ex. DX3 prove his settled possession.

Merely because the sale deed mentions that the property is under acquisition does not ipso facto lead to the conclusion that the said property was acquired pursuant to documents Ex.DW1/1, Ex.DW1/2 and Ex.DW1/3 especially in the absence of any corroborating material to show that the suit property falls within khasra no. 4/1/4.
62.
It is vehemently argued that since the land already stood acquired in 1961, the plaintiff could at best only be an encroacher on the government land and no injunction could Page no.20 of 29 RCA DJ No. 3/2016 Kanhaiya Lal v. Khairati Lal & Others have been granted against the true owner of the land.
Onus of proof of this issue was rightly placed on defendant no. 6, and it was its burden to lead cogent and reliable evidence to demolish/disprove the documents put forward by the plaintiff to tilt the scale of probabilities in its favor.
However, defendant no.6 failed to do so.
65. Defendant no.6, though claims that suit land was acquired, it failed to produce the site plan showing exact boundaries of the acquired land.
It is pertinent to note that DDA is a statutory body that is responsible for urban planning and land regulation.
It has the responsibility as well as the wherewithal to maintain authoritative records with respect to land classification, ownership and status.
In these circumstances, DDA was seized with the best evidence to prove the location of the suit property.
However, it failed to bring any conclusive evidence in this regard before the court.
66. There is also nothing on record that indicates that DDA ever took possession of suit land.
On the contrary, defendant's witnesses themselves have admitted the possession of the plaintiff on the suit land.
In similar circumstances, adverse findings were recorded against the DDA by the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in Tilak Raj Aggarwal & Ors. v. DDA1.
Further, it is not the case here that plaintiff has encroached the land rather revenue record Ex.DX3 shows that plaintiff came in possession of the suit land having purchased it from previous owner.
Registered sale document Ex.PW2/1 in his favour is also duly proved.
72. During the course of arguments, it was contended by ld. counsel for defendant no.6 that Ex.PW2/1 is not a sale deed but merely an agreement to sell as the sale was not complete, and only part consideration had been paid, while remaining was to 1 Judgment dated 16.01.2009 by the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in CS (OS) No. 2091/1993.
Page no.24 of 29 RCA DJ No. 3/2016 Kanhaiya Lal v. Khairati Lal & Others be paid subsequently once the land had been released from acquisition.
While there is force in the argument, it needs to be borne in mind that this is not a suit for declaration of title of ownership over the suit land, but simiplicitor suit for injunction.
Page no.25 of 29 RCA DJ No. 3/2016 Kanhaiya Lal v. Khairati Lal & Others committed, or is of a flimsy character, or recurring, intermittent, stray or casual in nature, or has just been committed, while the rightful owner did not have enough time to have recourse to law.
A stray act of trespass, or a possession which has not matured into settled possession, can be obstructed or removed by the true owner even by using necessary force.
The 'settled possession'
must be (i) effective, (ii) undisturbed, and (iii) to the knowledge of the owner or without any attempt at concealment by the trespasser.
Applying the aforesaid legal principles to the present case and seeking guidance therefrom, here plaintiff is not a trespasser or got possession of the land for a short duration, rather, he has relied upon a sale-deed to substantiate his right over suit land since 1966.
Ex.PW2/1 is a duly registered document, pursuant to which plaintiff came into possession of the suit property.
There was no attempt on part of plaintiff to conceal his possession.
Also, his possession is for a fairly long period and undisturbed.
Thus, possession of the plaintiff over the suit land is settled and he can only be evicted by following due process of law and not otherwise.
